findings.what: drainForever catches only InterruptedException. Any RuntimeException or Error escaping timer.awaitWindowClose() -- and WindowTimer is a PUBLIC seam taken by a public constructor, so third-party implementations are the intended case -- kills the committer thread. `running` stays true, so commit() keeps accepting requests; nothing ever completes the batch the dead thread was holding, and Pending.await() blocks on CompletableFuture.join(), which is uninterruptible. The class javadoc's claim that 'every batch is completed or failed by the thread that took it' is false on this path, and there is no supervision, restart, or way for a caller to observe the death.
findings.failure_scenario: MEASURED on the staged tree: new BatchingSequencer(delegate, () -> { throw new IllegalStateException(); }) then commit(req) had not returned after 5 s and cannot be interrupted. In production the same shape is any unchecked throw from a timer, or an Error (OOM) from the un-guarded `new ArrayList<>` in commitBatch: the ingester's flusher thread parks forever holding DefaultIngest's lock, every producer appending to that pod blocks behind it, and the pod is dead until SIGKILL while its readiness probe still passes. DefaultIngest:420-422 already records exactly this lesson -- 'a Pending nobody completes is a producer thread hung until SIGKILL'.

findings.what: commit() reads `running` at :93 and enqueues at :96 with no re-check afterwards, while close() at :197 sets running=false, interrupts and drains the queue exactly ONCE. A caller that observes running==true and is then descheduled before queue.add() enqueues after close()'s drainRemaining() has already run and after the committer has already returned from drainForever -- so the request is neither in a batch nor drainable by anyone, and its caller blocks forever on the uninterruptible join(). This is the precise window the close() javadoc promises does not exist ('A caller blocked in commit when close arrives must not wait for a window that will never close').
findings.failure_scenario: MEASURED on the staged tree: 24 concurrent callers racing one close() orphaned a caller within 102 attempts (still blocked 2 s later, count=1 outstanding). In production this is DefaultIngest.close() -> sequencer.close() racing the flusher thread's last commit: the shutdown path hangs on a thread that will never be completed, the pod misses its terminationGracePeriod and is SIGKILLed, and the lease is never voluntarily released -- turning a millisecond failover into a TTL-bound one (~10 s, ADR-0007), which is the exact cost the Sequencer contract says close() exists to avoid. Fix: re-check `running` after queue.add and fail-drain, or have close() drain in a loop until it observes the queue empty with the committer terminated.

findings.what: close() interrupts the committer and immediately calls delegate.close() without ever joining it, despite the javadoc claiming it 'STOPS THE COMMITTER, THEN THE DELEGATE'. It only signals; it never waits. So delegate.close() runs while the committer may still be inside delegate.commitAll(), i.e. inside CommitLog's redrive loop. Two consequences. (a) With LocalSequencer as delegate -- the delegate this class exists to wrap -- close() releases the LEASE while that PUT is still in flight; LocalSequencer.commitAll's `closed` guard was passed before close, so nothing stops it (and `closed` is a plain non-volatile boolean, which this commit is what first makes written on one thread and read on another). (b) The interrupt lands on a thread that may be mid-PUT; a store client on interruptible channels turns that into an IOException, which the Sequencer contract defines as the AMBIGUOUS case.
findings.failure_scenario: (a) Pod A shuts down. Its committer is redriving a lost CAS at slot N+1; close() releases the lease; pod B acquires epoch E+1, seals A's chain and starts committing. A's redrive then wins slot N+2 and lands a delta past the seal in a chain nobody fences -- the fork LocalSequencer's own javadoc says must not exist, assigning offsets B has already assigned (I2). (b) Every graceful shutdown under load manufactures an ambiguous conditional PUT whose caller cannot know whether it landed, which is precisely the case M4.10 does not yet make safe. Fix: committer.join() (bounded) before delegate.close().

findings.what: The commitAll() pass-through leaves the interface's own PRIMITIVE unbatched and runs the delegate on the caller's thread. (a) COST: Sequencer.java:96-111 now declares commitAll THE PRIMITIVE and commit merely its one-request default, on the stated grounds that 'an interface whose primitive is one-at-a-time makes the batched path the exception rather than the rule' -- but in the one implementation that batches, the primitive does not batch at all. Every submission arriving through commitAll is its own conditional PUT, so on that path the commit-chain PUT rate is one per submitting caller, i.e. it scales with PODS, which AC9 forbids by name ('does not change when the workload goes from 1 pod to 6'). M5's forwarding path -- a remote pod's already-grouped flushes arriving at the leaseholder -- is exactly a commitAll, so the shape that restores the per-pod rate is the shape M5 naturally takes. The javadoc's defence conflates ONE caller's grouping with the fleet-wide grouping the $52/month depends on. (b) CORRECTNESS: CommitLog is single-writer by construction (plain HashMap nextOffsets, plain long nextSequence, no synchronization, CommitLog.java:45-46), and the dedicated committer thread is what makes that safe. This pass-through invokes delegate.commitAll concurrently with the committer's own. (c) It also skips the `running` check commit() has.
findings.failure_scenario: (a) Six pods forward grouped flushes to the leaseholder's BatchingSequencer via commitAll: 6 PUTs per window instead of 1, restoring the per-pod commit rate this class exists to remove, silently and only in the multi-pod deployment nothing tests. (b) A caller thread in commitAll and the committer thread both run CommitLog.commitSubmissions: with no happens-before on nextOffsets, both read base=100 for the same RunKey and write deltas at different slots each claiming records 100..199 -- two segments claiming one offset range, which is I2 and which NO conditional write catches because each entry is written once and is internally consistent. A concurrent HashMap resize can also corrupt the map outright. No test covers a concurrent commitAll. Either batch commitAll into the window too, or state and enforce the bound (refuse it, or serialise it through the committer).

findings.what: M4.7a's backlog row assigns this to M4.7 in as many words: 'DefaultIngest still reads runs(), so it will THROW rather than mis-attribute the moment M4.7 batches -- deliberately loud, and M4.7 owns settling how a caller learns which offsets are its own.' The staged diff ships the batcher and leaves DefaultIngest:353 calling delta.runs(), which CommitDelta.only() refuses with IllegalStateException for any delta naming more than one segment. M4.7b settled the attribution RULE in the contract (match on the submitted segment key) but the only production caller of the seam was never moved onto it, and no test anywhere wires BatchingSequencer under DefaultIngest -- grep shows BatchingSequencer is referenced only by its own test. So the deliverable is a class that cannot be placed under the caller it exists for, and the row is marked done with the landmine it named still armed.
findings.failure_scenario: Assemble DefaultIngest over BatchingSequencer over LocalSequencer -- the arrangement the class exists for -- with any second contributor in the window. delegate.commitAll returns a durable two-segment delta; DefaultIngest:353 throws IllegalStateException('this delta batches 2 segments'); flushLocked's catch completes every waiting append exceptionally and rethrows. The producer is told its write FAILED for records whose offsets are already committed and durable, so it retries and duplicates them -- and because a single DefaultIngest holds its own lock across sequencer.commit, a single-pod test can never produce a second segment in a window, so nothing in the suite would ever go red.

findings.what: The fake advances its state before the refusal, where the real log refuses first and assigns nothing. `new CommitDelta(nextSequence++, segments)` increments nextSequence, and the loop above has already advanced nextOffsets for every request, by the time CommitDelta's compact constructor rejects a duplicate segment key. CommitLog.commitSubmissions validates the whole batch up front (duplicate keys AND empty recordCounts) and mutates nothing on refusal. The fake also does not carry the duplicate-key check itself, so it refuses with a different message than the contract's -- the class javadoc says the fake 'honours the same contract the interface states'.
findings.failure_scenario: A test asserts that a duplicate-key batch is refused against FakeSequencer, then commits a valid batch: the fake returns sequence 1 with offsets already advanced past the refused batch's counts, where the real sequencer would return sequence 0 at offset 0. The test either encodes the fake's phantom advance as expected behaviour or passes while the real implementation would not -- 'a fake that quietly differs is worse than no fake at all', which the file's own javadoc says.
